groups.title: Systems
groups.definition: The language exists to control memory and hardware directly: a runtime is optional, and layout is the programmer's business.

groups.title: Application
groups.definition: The language's main business is building general application software, with a managed runtime or a rich standard library.

groups.title: Web
groups.definition: The language's centre of gravity is the browser or the HTTP request and response model.

groups.title: Data and Science
groups.definition: The language's primary object is a dataset or a numeric array, not a program loop.

groups.title: Shells and Automation
groups.definition: The language's work is to drive a system: issuing commands, processing text streams, and gluing other programs together. Some members are interactive command interpreters; Perl is not, and belongs by the work, not the mechanism.

groups.title: Embedded and Real-Time
groups.definition: The language targets bare hardware, fixed timing, or a certification regime for a safety-critical system.

groups.title: Verification and Proof
groups.definition: The language's purpose is to make a machine check a claim about a program.

groups.title: Legacy and Retro
groups.definition: The language is retained for systems already written in it; new work in it is the exception.

groups.title: Education
groups.definition: The language exists mainly to teach programming.

groups.title: Blockchain
groups.definition: The language compiles to a chain's execution model.
